label: rem:kelvin-dispersion-derivation-steps
title: Derivation of the Kelvin dispersion from the $q$-Laplacian eigenvalue problem
html:
Setup. Let \varrho describe a stable vortex filament of length L in the brane fluid, parametrised by arc length s \in [0, L] under periodic boundary conditions \varrho(0) = \varrho(L). Let \eta(s, t) denote a small normal displacement of the filament from equilibrium (a Kelvin wave). The linearised q-Navier--Stokes equation governing normal perturbations of \varrho reads

  \partial_t^2 \eta
  = 
  \frac{\Gamma_q}{4\pi a_q^2}\Delta_q\eta
  -  \nu_q\Delta_q\partial_t \eta,

where \Gamma_q = [j]_q[j+1]_q fixes the quantised circulation at intensity level j, a_q specifies the q-deformed vortex core radius, and the trailing term applies viscous damping.

The q-Laplacian eigenvalue problem. The q-Laplacian evaluated on a circle of length L acts exclusively on L-periodic functions f(s). Its eigenvalue problem reads

  \Delta_qf_k
  =  -\mu_kf_k,
  \qquad
  f_k(s + L) = f_k(s).

For the classical Laplacian (q = 1) in arc length s, the eigenfunctions are e^{2\pi i k s / L} with eigenvalues \mu_k = (2\pi k/L)^2. The q-Laplacian replaces the integer k with the q-integer [k]_q = (q^k - q^{-k})/(q - q^{-1}). The derivation below works in the variable z = e^{2\pi i s / L}, where the eigenvalue is the dimensionless

  \mu_k^{(q)}
  = 
  [k]_q^2 .

The arc-length factor (2\pi/L)^2 is a change of unit, not part of the algebraic operator. All units are restored at once by the single factor \hbar_q / L_q^2 below. So L_q is the length in that normalisation: matching \hbar_q times the arc-length eigenvalue (2\pi[k]_q/L)^2 sets L_q = L/(2\pi), whereas writing (2\pi[k]_q/L_q)^2 at L_q = L would differ from \lambda_k^{(q)} below by the factor 4\pi^2/\hbar_q.

Derivation. The q-derivative operators define the q-Laplacian. Assign z = e^{2\pi i s / L} for a function f on the circle. Then:

  D_q f(z) = \frac{f(qz) - f(q^{-1}z)}{(q - q^{-1})z},

and \Delta_q = -zD_q \circ zD_q (composing the radial part of the q-Casimir). Operating on the monomial z^k yields

  D_q(z^k)
  = \frac{q^k z^k - q^{-k} z^k}{(q - q^{-1})z}
  = [k]_qz^{k-1}.

Consequently zD_q(z^k) = [k]_qz^k, proving

  \Delta_q(z^k) = -[k]_q^2z^k.

The exact eigenvalue reads \mu_k^{(q)} = [k]_q^2. Restoring physical units (filament length L_q and quantum of action \hbar_q) produces:

  \lambda_k^{(q)}
  = 
  [k]_q^2 \cdot \frac{\hbar_q}{L_q^2}.

This precisely matches the formula declared in the discrete vortex spectrum.

Dispersion relation. Inserting \eta(s,t) = f_k(s)e^{-i\omega t} into the linearised equation and applying \Delta_q f_k = -[k]_q^2 f_k / L_q^2 yields

  -\omega^2
  = 
  -\frac{\Gamma_q}{4\pi a_q^2}\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}
  +  i\omega\nu_q\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}.

In the undamped limit (\nu_q = 0, tracing the Euler limit), the dispersion relation simplifies to

  \omega_k^{(q)}
  = 
  \frac{\Gamma_q^{1/2}}{2\sqrt{\pi}a_q}
  \frac{[k]_q}{L_q},

producing the q-deformed Kelvin dispersion. In the damped regime (\nu_q > 0), the complex frequency isolates the decay rate

  \gamma_k^{(q)}
  = 
  \frac{\nu_q}{2}\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}
  = 
  \frac{\hbar_q}{4}\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}.

Mode k decays on the timescale \tau_k = 1/\gamma_k^{(q)} = 4L_q^2 / (\hbar_q[k]_q^2). Because [k]_q \sim q^k at large k, high modes decay doubly exponentially in k. This generates the rigorous exponential UV cutoff built into the q-Navier--Stokes definition.
